notes.front: What is a contingency procedure in small UAS operations?
notes.back: Your planned action if a hazard still occurs despite your mitigations.
notes.explanation: Emergency and contingency procedures are planned before flight and briefed to the crew, so nobody improvises under pressure.
notes.example: If the control link is lost: try to re-establish it; if that fails, start the planned lost-link procedure.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶A.4 note (4), p. A-5

notes.front: Why are lithium-based batteries a hazard in small UAS operations?
notes.back: They are highly flammable and capable of ignition, and a battery fire can cause loss of control in flight.
notes.explanation: Many small UA run on lithium batteries, so safe handling, charging and use are part of every operation.
notes.example: A battery damaged in a hard landing may later catch fire on the bench or in the air.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: What is thermal runaway in a lithium battery?
notes.back: Overheating in which a cell releases burning lithium or the flammable liquid inside it (electrolyte), driving neighbouring cells into runaway too.
notes.explanation: It explains why a lithium fire can flare up again and again, and why cooling matters after the flames are out.
notes.example: Like a row of dominoes: one overheated cell topples the next.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 09013, “Fighting Fires Caused By Lithium Type Batteries in Portable Electronic Devices” (23 June 2009)

notes.front: What is a lost link in small UAS operations?
notes.back: Loss of the control link between the control station and the small unmanned aircraft.
notes.explanation: Without the link the pilot cannot command the aircraft, so a lost-link procedure must be planned and briefed before flight.
notes.example: Flying behind a building, or near many Wi-Fi signals, can break the link.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶A.4, Figure A-2, p. A-4

notes.front: What is an unlicensed frequency band, as used by most small UAS?
notes.back: A radio band, such as 2.4 GHz or 5.8 GHz, that can be used without an individual FCC licence.
notes.explanation: Because anyone may use these bands, including Wi-Fi networks, the aircraft’s link can suffer interference.
notes.example: Your drone and your neighbour’s Wi-Fi router may share the 2.4 GHz band.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.6.1, p. B-3

notes.front: Before flight the remote PIC must make sure everyone directly participating knows the operating conditions, roles and responsibilities, potential hazards, contingency procedures and {{c1::emergency procedures}}.
notes.explanation: The preflight briefing is where emergency planning reaches the crew.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.49 “Preflight familiarization, inspection, and actions for aircraft operation” (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Which crew members must be briefed on the planned emergency procedures?
notes.back: All of them, including any visual observers and any non-certificated person allowed to manipulate the controls.
notes.explanation: Everyone who might have to act in an emergency needs to know the plan in advance.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 5, p. 35

notes.front: In the study guide’s example, a small UA has a battery fire in flight. What may the remote pilot do?
notes.back: Climb above 400 feet AGL if needed to reach a safe landing area, reporting only if the FAA asks.
notes.explanation: In an emergency the remote pilot may deviate from part 107 to the extent needed to avoid harming people or property.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 5, p. 35

notes.front: After deviating from a part 107 rule in an in-flight emergency, when must the remote PIC send a written report?
notes.back: Only when the Administrator (the FAA) requests it.
notes.explanation: The deviation is allowed only to the extent necessary to meet the emergency.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.21 “In-flight emergency” (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: In the AC’s accident-scene example, what does the remote PIC plan in case the take-off site is taken by an EMS helicopter while power runs low?
notes.back: An alternate landing site, and possibly sites where the aircraft can be sacrificed without risk to people or manned aircraft.
notes.explanation: Thinking through “what if?” before flight turns a surprise into a planned contingency.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶A.4.8.1, p. A-7

notes.front: AC 107-2A says lithium battery fires can be caused by {{c1::short circuits}}, improper charging, heating to extreme temperatures, damage from a crash, mishandling and simple defects.
notes.explanation: Knowing every cause tells you what to avoid when charging, carrying, flying and storing batteries.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: AC 107-2A says lithium battery fires can be caused by short circuits, {{c1::improper charging}}, heating to extreme temperatures, damage from a crash, mishandling and simple defects.
notes.explanation: Knowing every cause tells you what to avoid when charging, carrying, flying and storing batteries.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: AC 107-2A says lithium battery fires can be caused by short circuits, improper charging, {{c1::heating to extreme temperatures}}, damage from a crash, mishandling and simple defects.
notes.explanation: Knowing every cause tells you what to avoid when charging, carrying, flying and storing batteries.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: AC 107-2A says lithium battery fires can be caused by short circuits, improper charging, heating to extreme temperatures, {{c1::damage from a crash}}, mishandling and simple defects.
notes.explanation: Knowing every cause tells you what to avoid when charging, carrying, flying and storing batteries.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: AC 107-2A says lithium battery fires can be caused by short circuits, improper charging, heating to extreme temperatures, damage from a crash, {{c1::mishandling}} and simple defects.
notes.explanation: Knowing every cause tells you what to avoid when charging, carrying, flying and storing batteries.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: AC 107-2A says lithium battery fires can be caused by short circuits, improper charging, heating to extreme temperatures, damage from a crash, mishandling and {{c1::simple defects}}.
notes.explanation: Knowing every cause tells you what to avoid when charging, carrying, flying and storing batteries.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: What does AC 107-2A advise remote PICs to follow for safe lithium battery handling and use?
notes.back: The manufacturer’s recommendations, when available.
notes.explanation: Safe charging and usage limits are set by the battery and aircraft maker.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: Why can a lithium battery fire flare up repeatedly?
notes.back: Each cell in thermal runaway heats its neighbours, so cells rupture one after another, each releasing its contents.
notes.explanation: Putting out the flames does not stop the remaining cells heating up.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 09013, “Fighting Fires Caused By Lithium Type Batteries in Portable Electronic Devices” (23 June 2009)

notes.front: What does SAFO 09013 recommend for extinguishing a lithium battery fire in a portable device?
notes.back: A Halon (a type of fire extinguisher), Halon-replacement or water extinguisher.
notes.explanation: That puts out the fire and stops it spreading; cooling comes next.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 09013, “Fighting Fires Caused By Lithium Type Batteries in Portable Electronic Devices” (23 June 2009)

notes.front: After a lithium battery fire is out, what does SAFO 09013 recommend next?
notes.back: Douse the device with water or another non-alcoholic liquid to cool it.
notes.explanation: Cooling stops more cells from reaching thermal runaway.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 09013, “Fighting Fires Caused By Lithium Type Batteries in Portable Electronic Devices” (23 June 2009)

notes.front: What does SAFO 09013 warn against doing with a smoking or burning lithium-powered device?
notes.back: Picking it up or moving it, and covering it or cooling it with ice.
notes.explanation: Ice and covers insulate the device, making further thermal runaway more likely; handling it can injure you.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 09013, “Fighting Fires Caused By Lithium Type Batteries in Portable Electronic Devices” (23 June 2009)

notes.front: Travelling by airline, may you pack spare lithium batteries in checked baggage?
notes.back: No; spare lithium batteries are prohibited in checked baggage, including bags checked at the gate.
notes.explanation: Limited exceptions allow spare batteries for personal use in carry-on baggage (49 CFR 175.10).
notes.source: FAA SAFO 15010, “Carriage of Spare Lithium Batteries in Carry-on and Checked Baggage” (8 October 2015)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · SAFO 15010 (8 Oct 2015), listed on the FAA SAFO page on that date

notes.front: How must each spare lithium battery in carry-on baggage be protected?
notes.back: Individually, against short circuits: original packaging, taped terminals, or its own plastic bag or pouch.
notes.explanation: Short circuits are one of the listed causes of lithium battery fires.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 15010, “Carriage of Spare Lithium Batteries in Carry-on and Checked Baggage” (8 October 2015)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · SAFO 15010 (8 Oct 2015), listed on the FAA SAFO page on that date

notes.front: What must spare lithium batteries not touch in carry-on baggage?
notes.back: Metal objects such as coins, keys or jewellery; also prevent crushing, puncturing or pressure on them.
notes.explanation: Metal can bridge the terminals and cause a short circuit.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 15010, “Carriage of Spare Lithium Batteries in Carry-on and Checked Baggage” (8 October 2015)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · SAFO 15010 (8 Oct 2015), listed on the FAA SAFO page on that date

notes.front: In the AC’s sample risk assessment, what is the contingency procedure for a lost control link?
notes.back: Try to re-establish the link; if that fails, start the emergency or contingency procedures for loss of control link.
notes.explanation: The mitigation beforehand is a control link check and a preflight briefing that covers link loss.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶A.4, Figure A-2, p. A-4

notes.front: What causes of a lost control link does the AC’s sample risk assessment list?
notes.back: Loss of power from the control station, the aircraft out of range, and interference from another device (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth).
notes.explanation: Each cause suggests a mitigation: power checks, staying within range, and avoiding crowded radio environments.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶A.4, Figure A-2, p. A-4

notes.front: What must the remote PIC confirm about control links before flight?
notes.back: That all control links between the ground control station and the small unmanned aircraft are working properly.
notes.explanation: This preflight check is the first defence against a lost link.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.49 “Preflight familiarization, inspection, and actions for aircraft operation” (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: If the remote PIC loses sight of the aircraft and cannot regain VLOS, what should they follow?
notes.back: Pre-determined loss-of-VLOS procedures, such as landing immediately, hovering, or a return-to-home sequence.
notes.explanation: Which option is right depends on the capabilities of the small UAS.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.9, p. 5-6

notes.front: What should a preflight check confirm about GPS?
notes.back: That the small UAS has acquired GPS location from the minimum number of satellites the manufacturer specifies.
notes.explanation: Checking before launch reduces the chance of losing position information in flight.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 10, p. 7-3

notes.front: Which two unlicensed bands do most small UAS use for the control station–aircraft link?
notes.back: 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz.
notes.explanation: 900 MHz is also unlicensed; other frequencies need a user-specific FCC licence.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.6.1, p. B-3

notes.front: Why can flying among dense housing and office buildings cause link problems?
notes.back: The 2.4 and 5.8 GHz bands are also used by wireless computer networks, and their interference can cause loss of control and flyaways.
notes.explanation: Your control link and the networks use the same frequencies, so interference can stop the aircraft hearing your commands.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.6.1, p. B-3

notes.front: To avoid interference, how do many modern small UAS split their two bands?
notes.back: 5.8 GHz to control the aircraft and 2.4 GHz to send video and photos to the ground.
notes.explanation: Check the operating manual for your own aircraft’s arrangement.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.6.1.1, p. B-3

notes.front: What happens to a 2.4 or 5.8 GHz control link if a barrier comes between control station and aircraft?
notes.back: It will not work properly: both bands are line of sight.
notes.explanation: Keeping VLOS, which part 107 requires, also helps keep obstructions out of the radio path.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.6.1.2, p. B-3

notes.front: Which agency authorises civil use of the radio frequencies that control small UAS?
notes.back: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC).
notes.explanation: Unlicensed bands (900 MHz, 2.4 GHz, 5.8 GHz) need no FCC approval; other frequencies need a licence.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.6.2, p. B-3

notes.front: Before flight, which contingency must the crew be briefed on for people or vehicles not directly participating?
notes.back: What to do if they enter the operational area.
notes.explanation: This is part of the preflight briefing and is central to operations over people.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.11.1 item 2, p. 5-10

notes.front: Before an operation over people, what must the remote PIC confirm about the aircraft?
notes.back: That it is eligible for the category of operation (meets §107.110, §107.120(a), §107.130(a) or §107.140).
notes.explanation: Eligibility is a preflight action, not something to check once people are underneath.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.49 “Preflight familiarization, inspection, and actions for aircraft operation” (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: In almost all night operations, what may the remote PIC need to do to the operational area?
notes.back: Restrict it, so the aircraft stays within the intended area and within VLOS.
notes.explanation: Reduced lighting and contrast make it hard to judge the aircraft’s position, attitude and direction at night.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.9.3, p. 5-7

notes.front: Planning a night flight near unlit towers and buildings, what hazard does the AC tell you to consider?
notes.back: Your eyes may not have adjusted to the dark (night vision adaptation), so unlit towers and buildings are hard to see.
notes.explanation: The AC also asks whether weather and terrain will stop other aircraft seeing the anti-collision light for 3 statute miles.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶A.4 (a) item 6, p. A-5

notes.front: At 350 feet AGL your aircraft reports a battery fire. The only clear landing area is past a crowd, and the safest route means climbing to 450 feet AGL. What may you do?
notes.back: Climb above 400 feet AGL to reach the safe landing area; report the deviation only if the FAA asks.
notes.choices:
A) Stay below 400 feet and land among the crowd
B) Climb as needed to reach the safe area; report if asked
C) Climb, then file a written report within 10 days
notes.choicesExplained: A: rules may be broken to the extent needed to avoid harming people. C: a written report of the deviation is only needed on FAA request; it is not an automatic 10-day report.
notes.explanation: An in-flight emergency allows deviating from part 107 as far as needed to avoid a hazard to people or property.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide, FAA-G-8082-22 (2016), ch. 5, p. 35

notes.front: Your visual observer arrives after your briefing and says, “Just tell me where to stand.” What else must you cover before flying?
notes.back: The emergency and contingency procedures, plus operating conditions, roles and hazards.
notes.explanation: Every person directly participating must be informed before flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.49 “Preflight familiarization, inspection, and actions for aircraft operation” (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: You are hired to film a block of flats with dozens of Wi-Fi networks. Your aircraft uses 2.4 and 5.8 GHz. What risk should your plan address?
notes.back: Radio interference causing loss of control or a flyaway.
notes.explanation: Those bands are shared with wireless networks; plan link checks and a lost-link procedure.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.6.1, p. B-3

notes.front: You plan to send the aircraft round the far side of a warehouse, out of sight, “just for a second”. Besides breaking VLOS, what else is at risk?
notes.back: The control link: 2.4 and 5.8 GHz are line of sight and will not work properly through the building.
notes.explanation: VLOS and a clear radio path go together.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.6.1.2, p. B-3

notes.front: Mid-flight, the control station shows “link lost”. According to the AC’s sample plan, what is your first action?
notes.back: Try to re-establish the control link; if you cannot, start the planned lost-link procedure.
notes.explanation: The sample contingency is re-establish first, then emergency or contingency procedures.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶A.4, Figure A-2, p. A-4

notes.front: A sudden glare makes you lose sight of the aircraft and you cannot find it again. What should you do?
notes.back: Follow your pre-determined loss-of-VLOS procedure, such as land, hover or return-to-home, as the aircraft allows.
notes.explanation: Choose the option the aircraft’s capabilities support; decide it before flight, not during.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.9, p. 5-6

notes.front: At preflight, the app shows fewer GPS satellites than the manufacturer’s minimum. What should you do?
notes.back: Do not launch yet; wait until the aircraft has acquired GPS from at least the specified minimum.
notes.explanation: The AC’s preflight items include verifying GPS lock from the manufacturer’s minimum number of satellites.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶7.3.4 item 10, p. 7-3

notes.front: Flying to a job by airline, you plan to put four spare drone batteries, loose, in your checked suitcase. What is wrong?
notes.back: Spare lithium batteries may not go in checked baggage; carry them on, each protected against short circuit.
notes.explanation: Tape the terminals or use original packaging or individual bags, away from metal objects.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 15010, “Carriage of Spare Lithium Batteries in Carry-on and Checked Baggage” (8 October 2015)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · SAFO 15010 (8 Oct 2015), listed on the FAA SAFO page on that date

notes.front: A charging battery on your bench starts smoking and catches fire. A colleague reaches to throw it outside. What does SAFO 09013 advise?
notes.back: Do not pick it up; extinguish it (Halon extinguisher or water) and then douse it with water to cool it.
notes.explanation: Moving a burning device risks injury; cooling stops more cells going into thermal runaway.
notes.source: FAA SAFO 09013, “Fighting Fires Caused By Lithium Type Batteries in Portable Electronic Devices” (23 June 2009)

notes.front: A battery pack was dropped on concrete last week and its case is dented. Which of the AC’s listed fire causes does this fit?
notes.back: Damage from a crash or mishandling.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A lists crash damage and mishandling among the causes of lithium battery fires.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: To save time you charge your drone batteries with a faster third-party charger that does not match the manufacturer’s instructions. Which listed fire cause are you risking?
notes.back: Improper charging.
notes.explanation: Follow the manufacturer’s recommendations for charging and use.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: You leave spare batteries on the dashboard of a closed car in summer sun all afternoon. Which listed cause of lithium battery fires are you risking?
notes.back: Heating to extreme temperatures.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A lists extreme heat among the causes of lithium battery fires.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: A loose spare battery rattles around in a bag with your car keys and coins. Which listed cause of lithium battery fires are you risking?
notes.back: A short circuit.
notes.explanation: Metal objects can bridge the terminals; spare batteries should be individually protected.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: You prise a stuck battery out of the aircraft with a screwdriver, gouging its casing. Which listed cause of lithium battery fires does this fit?
notes.back: Mishandling.
notes.explanation: AC 107-2A lists mishandling alongside crash damage among the causes.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: A brand-new, never-damaged battery overheats on its first correct charge. Which listed cause of lithium battery fires is most likely?
notes.back: The battery is simply defective.
notes.explanation: Even a correctly handled battery can fail if it is defective.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.5, p. B-3

notes.front: During a filming job, a jogger runs into your operational area. Your aircraft is not eligible for operations over people. What should already exist?
notes.back: A contingency procedure, briefed before flight, for non-participants entering the area.
notes.explanation: The preflight briefing must include contingency procedures for people or vehicles entering the operational area.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.11.1 item 2, p. 5-10

notes.front: You plan a night roof inspection using the same wide area you use by day. What does the AC suggest you reconsider?
notes.back: Restricting the operational area so you can keep the aircraft in VLOS and within the intended area.
notes.explanation: At night reduced contrast makes position and direction hard to judge; the anti-collision light alone is not enough.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.9.3, p. 5-7

notes.front: Emergency deviation report versus safety event report: which is sent only if the FAA asks?
notes.back: The emergency deviation report (§107.21); a safety event meeting §107.9’s thresholds must be reported within 10 calendar days regardless.
notes.explanation: The two duties are separate; one event can trigger both.
notes.source: 14 CFR 107.21 “In-flight emergency” (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Lost link versus loss of VLOS: which one means you can see the aircraft but cannot command it?
notes.back: Lost link; loss of VLOS means you can command it but cannot see it.
notes.explanation: Each needs its own pre-planned procedure.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.9; A.4, Figure A-2, p. 5-6
